note: Hand-curated source classification for WortHogg. This file is the authority on WHAT a source is; data/sources/registry.json is generated from it plus a scan of the datasets (app/build-sources.mjs) and records WHERE each source is used. Two layers: `publishers` classifies every citable host once, and `documents` upgrades specific URLs that have been individually checked. The generator refuses to classify a host that is not listed here, so adding a new citation to a new domain is a deliberate act.

reliabilityRules.primary: The organisation that measured or legislated the figure, publishing it itself: manufacturer technical data sheets, government standards and regulations, nutrition labels, peer-reviewed primary research, standards bodies.
reliabilityRules.secondary: Competent parties reporting or synthesising others' measurements: review papers, extension services, trade associations, club guides, practitioner reference tools.
reliabilityRules.tertiary: General reference works. Useful orientation, never adequate to support a numeric specification in this project.

citationRules.numericClaim: A record carrying numeric specifications must cite at least one source with reliability primary or secondary AND deepLink true. A tertiary source, or a bare publisher homepage, can never support a number.
citationRules.qualitativeClaim: Descriptive text may rest on any source, including tertiary, provided the source is named.
citationRules.verification: full-text means the document was retrieved and the figures read out of it. metadata-only means the document's existence and title were confirmed but the figures were taken from a search summary or abstract. unverified means neither — the citation is inherited from earlier work and has not been checked.

documents.title: WildBrew Sour Pitch — Technical Data Sheet
documents.supports: Lactobacillus plantarum, facultative hetero-fermentative; 30-40 °C (86-104 °F); final pH 3.2-3.5; dose 10 g/hL; >10^11 CFU/g; descriptors citrus, tangy, sour; unhopped wort; styles Berliner Weisse, Gose, lambic, American Wild, Sour IPA.
documents.doesNotSupport: Attenuation, alcohol tolerance, flocculation, or any IBU inhibition threshold.

documents.title: WildBrew Philly Sour — Technical Data Sheet
documents.supports: Lachancea thermotolerans, pure active dried strain; attenuation 74-82%; 20-30 °C (68-86 °F), optimal 25-30 °C (77-86 °F); flocculation high; alcohol tolerance 9% ABV; pitching 50-150 g/hL; viability >=1x10^9 CFU/g; POF negative; diastaticus negative; killer negative; aroma sour, red apple, stone fruit, peach; fermentation completable in 10 days at 20 °C.
documents.doesNotSupport: Species-wide behaviour of L. thermotolerans outside this product; titratable acidity figures are quoted in Lallemand standard-conditions wort only.

documents.title: The yeast Kluyveromyces marxianus and its biotechnological potential
documents.supports: Lactose assimilation and fermentation; thermotolerance with maximum growth temperature variously reported as 47 °C (Anderson et al. 1986), 49 °C (Hughes et al. 1984) and 52 °C (Banat et al. 1992); ethanol production above 40 °C; LOWER ethanol tolerance than S. cerevisiae, correlated with plasma-membrane ATPase activity (Rosa & Sá-Correia 1992); Crabtree-negative and facultatively fermentative; cannot grow under strictly anaerobic conditions, with ethanol formation almost exclusively linked to oxygen availability.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any single numeric alcohol tolerance for the species. The 10% v/v figure circulating for K. marxianus comes from strains after ~100 days of directed adaptive evolution and is not a native specification.

documents.title: Brewing Sour and Wild Ales (incl. 'The Falcon Method For Fermenting Lambics', credited to MB Raines)
documents.supports: Brettanomyces species characters — B. claussenii/anomalus (English stock beer origin, softer, pineapple and mango), B. bruxellensis (Brussels, medium earthy funk), B. lambicus (every lambic, huge horsey character with fruitiness, smoky and sour). Lactobacillus delbrueckii: lactic acid for crisp dry acidity, primary character of Berliner Weisse, ferment very warm e.g. 98 °F. Pediococcus: large lactic production from glucose, no CO2, massive diacetyl charge in early ferment. Acetobacter as 'vinegar mother' converting ethanol to acetic acid. Enterobacter contributing bilious characters. Timeline: at least a month before cultures show character, optimally six months to a year. Named blends WLP655, Wyeast 3278, Wyeast 3763 Roeselare.
documents.doesNotSupport: Temperature ranges, attenuation, flocculation or alcohol tolerance for any of these organisms except the single 98 °F figure for L. delbrueckii.

documents.title: 125th Anniversary Review: Bacteria in brewing — the good, the bad and the ugly
documents.publisher: Journal of the Institute of Brewing 118:335-345
documents.supports: Lactobacillus brevis and Pediococcus damnosus as the lactic acid bacteria most commonly implicated in beer spoilage; L. brevis among the most hop-tolerant; hop iso-alpha-acids as ionophores impairing proton motive force; beer typically carrying 17-55 ppm iso-alpha-acids as an intrinsic antimicrobial hurdle.
documents.doesNotSupport: Species-level temperature ranges, alcohol tolerances or per-species IBU inhibition thresholds. Figures here were read from abstract and search summaries, not the full text — verification is metadata-only.

documents.title: Review: Pure non-Saccharomyces starter cultures for beer fermentation with a focus on secondary metabolites and practical applications
documents.publisher: Journal of the Institute of Brewing 122:569-587
documents.supports: Saccharomycodes ludwigii does not ferment maltose or maltotriose and therefore yields low alcohol with desirable flavours; industrial production of alcohol-free beer with maltose-negative S. ludwigii; Torulaspora delbrueckii among non-Saccharomyces starters of brewing interest.
documents.doesNotSupport: Temperature ranges, attenuation or alcohol tolerance for these species. Verification is metadata-only.

documents.title: Notes from the Field: Botulism from Drinking Prison-Made Illicit Alcohol in Utah, 2011
documents.publisher: Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report 62(07):138, US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
documents.supports: An outbreak of foodborne botulism among prisoners who drank pruno; eight hospitalised; type A botulinum toxin identified; a weeks-old baked potato implicated as the spore source. Establishes pruno as a documented public-health hazard rather than folklore.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any production method, ingredient ratio or yield. This project cites it to describe and warn, not to instruct.

documents.title: Dampfbier, Bayerisch
documents.publisher: GradPlato — Fachverlag Hans Carl GmbH, Nürnberg
documents.supports: Historical Dampfbier as a top-fermented, medium-dark barley-malt beer of the Bayerischer Wald near the Bohemian border, popular toward the end of the 19th century and brewed predominantly in summer. Modern versions deep gold to light amber, medium body, hopped only very lightly to about 15 BE, low carbonation ('wenig Rezenz'), fermented fast and warm with ordinary Weissbier yeast at about 21 °C, giving a slightly phenolic and banana-like finish — 'quasi ein Weißbier ohne Weizen'. Name derived from the large foam bubbles thrown by a vigorous open-vessel primary fermentation, which looked as though the wort were giving off steam as each burst. May be filtered or unfiltered. One published recipe's targets: Stammwürze 12 °P, Restextrakt 2.5 °P, 14 BE, 10 EBC, 5.1 % alcohol by volume; Hallertauer Mittelfrüh at 4.25 % alpha for both bittering and aroma; infusion mash 67 °C/30 min, 72 °C/20 min, 76 °C for lautering; 60 min boil; ferment ~4 days at ~21 °C; krausen with reserved wort; spund at ~0.5 bar for a week, a further week under pressure, adjust to ~3.5 g/L CO2. Records that the Dampfbierbrauerei Zwiesel brews a Dampfbier to a historical recipe.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any style RANGE. Every figure above is a single formulation's target, not a measured minimum and maximum across the style, and no judging body catalogues Dampfbier for one to be taken from. Also does not support a malt bill: the page's percentage column is internally inconsistent — Pilsner 35 % / Münchner 1 25 % sums to 60 %, not the stated 100 %, while its kilogram column (2.71 + 1.16 = 3.87 kg) is self-consistent and implies roughly 70 % / 30 %. The percentages are therefore not transcribed into this project. The page is bylined 'Jule' and does NOT credit Horst Dornbusch; the shared publisher is circumstantial and is not treated as authorship.

documents.title: Stile mit Geschichte – Folge 16: Dampfbier – Wenn's in der Brauerei zischt und brodelt
documents.supports: Qualitative corroboration only, and only where it agrees with a better source: origin in Niederbayern and the Bayerischer Wald, where 19th-century brewers had little means of cooling and so treated top-fermented beer like lager; top-fermenting yeast worked unusually warm, often in open vessels, throwing a wild foaming fermentation that appeared to steam; the style nearly died out, kept alive by a few breweries (it names Hutthurmer and Lang-Bräu) and revived occasionally as a historical style; malt-forward, fruity-spicy, with some yeast character, neither heavy nor sweet; pale barley malt with small roast-malt additions, moderate regional hops such as Hallertauer, house top-fermenting strains, soft to medium-hard water. Also notes that Anchor Steam's warm-fermentation origin is a parallel response to the same lack of refrigeration and not a direct relation.
documents.doesNotSupport: Every number it prints. Unbylined and uncited, so tertiary, which in this project can never carry a numeric specification. Its 20-30 IBU and 4.8-5.2 % ABV figures are recorded in the style entry as a DISAGREEMENT with the Hans Carl recipe's 14 BE rather than averaged or merged into it.

documents.title: Horst Dornbusch — biography and bibliography
documents.publisher: horstdornbusch.com (author's own site); bibliography cross-checked against German Wikipedia
documents.supports: Horst Dornbusch, born 1947 in Düsseldorf, German-American brewing consultant, brewer and technical author; founder of Cerevisia Communications LLC; won a Great American Beer Festival bronze medal for an Altbier; Associate Editor and a major contributor to The Oxford Companion to Beer (Oxford University Press). His German beer-style works, whose ISBNs are the durable identifiers: 'Das große BRAUWELT Lexikon der Biersorten' (Fachverlag Hans Carl, Nürnberg, 2017, ISBN 978-3-418-00131-9) and 'Die Biersorten der BRAUWELT. Ihre Geschichten & Rezepturen' (Fachverlag Hans Carl, Nürnberg, ISBN 978-3-418-00126-5); in English, 'Prost! The Story of German Beer' (Brewers Publications, 1997, ISBN 978-0-937381-55-7), 'Altbier' (1998, ISBN 978-0-937381-62-5), 'Bavarian Helles' (2000, ISBN 978-0-937381-73-1), 'The Ultimate Almanac of World Beer Recipes' (2010, ISBN 978-0984444908), 'Beer Styles from Around the World' (2015, ISBN 978-0984444922).
documents.doesNotSupport: Any beer style specification whatsoever. Neither the site nor the Wikipedia article reproduces the germanbeerinstitute.com style pages, and the books' contents have not been consulted — this entry exists so the bibliography is on record as the place a future verification would have to go, not as a citation for any figure. Note also that German Wikipedia misprints the year of the 'Biersorten der BRAUWELT' edition as 1916.

documents.title: Das große BRAUWELT Lexikon der Biersorten (review)
documents.publisher: BRAUWELT 39-40, 2017, p. 1176 — Fachverlag Hans Carl, Nürnberg
documents.supports: That Horst Dornbusch authored 'Das große BRAUWELT Lexikon der Biersorten' (2017), an A-to-Z inventory of world beer styles from antiquity to the present covering classic styles, craft-era beers and the most significant historical styles, deliberately written with minimal brew-science vocabulary, and that the author explicitly claims no completeness.
documents.doesNotSupport: The contents of any individual entry in that book, Dampfbier included. This is a review, not the text.

documents.title: Yeast: The Practical Guide to Beer Fermentation
documents.publisher: Brewers Publications, Boulder CO (Brewing Elements series)
documents.supports: The canonical modern reference on brewing yeast and fermentation: pitch-rate theory, cell viability and vitality, starter propagation, yeast harvesting and repitching, fermentation temperature and health. ISBN-13 978-0-937381-96-0. This is the acknowledged literature basis, alongside the Maltose Falcons propagation guide, for this project's pitching-rate reconstruction in lib/pitching/formulas.ts.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any figure attributed to a specific page. The book's contents have not been opened in this environment — only its existence and bibliographic identity are confirmed — so verification is metadata-only and no numeric claim rests on it. The ISBN is the identifier a future page-level check would use. The numeric yeast specs this project ships are transcribed from the yeast producers' own spec sheets (White Labs, Wyeast, Lallemand, Omega, Fermentis), which are the primary measurements this book itself synthesises.

documents.title: Water: A Comprehensive Guide for Brewers
documents.publisher: Brewers Publications, Boulder CO (Brewing Elements series)
documents.supports: The comprehensive modern reference on brewing water: the function of each ion, residual alkalinity and its effect on mash pH, sulfate-to-chloride balance, source-water treatment, brewing-salt additions and sparge acidification. ISBN-13 978-0-937381-99-1. The framework behind this project's water-chemistry and mash-pH guidance (lib/water-salts.ts, lib/mash-ph.ts).

Municipal water ion figures in this project cite the utilities' own published analyses (with Bru'n Water as a secondary aggregate), and salt ion contributions are derived from each salt's molar mass, not taken from this book.

documents.title: Active Dry Wine Yeast (ADWY) rehydration
documents.supports: The professional wine-yeast inoculation standard: an inoculum of 0.25 g/L (25 g/hL) of active dry wine yeast to achieve a minimum 5×10^6 viable cells/mL; rehydrate by sprinkling over 5-10 times its weight of 38-40 C water and standing 10-15 minutes; up to about twice the dose for highly clarified, high-Brix or high-SO2 musts. Underpins the wine-cultured fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Beer/cider/mead pitch rates, or any wild-ferment figure. It is the wine active-dry-yeast standard specifically.

documents.title: The Microbial Diversity of Traditional Spontaneously Fermented Lambic Beer
documents.supports: The microbiology of spontaneous lambic fermentation, from over 2000 isolates sampled over two years at a traditional Belgian lambic brewery. No yeast is pitched: cooled overnight in an open coolship, the wort is inoculated by the ambient microbiota of the Senne valley, then matures 1-3 years before bottling. A characteristic succession follows: Enterobacteriaceae dominate the first month (~3-40 days), replaced at ~2 months by Pediococcus damnosus with Saccharomyces cerevisiae and S. pastorianus, then from ~6 months onward by the acid- and ethanol-tolerant Dekkera bruxellensis alongside P. damnosus. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0095384. Underpins the beer-spontaneous fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Pitch rates (there is no pitch), or the microbiota of any other region's spontaneous ferment; it documents traditional Belgian lambic specifically.

documents.title: Sustainable Production of African Traditional Beers With Focus on Dolo, a West African Sorghum-Based Alcoholic Beverage
documents.supports: The microbiology of West African sorghum opaque beer (dolo, pito): a two-stage spontaneous fermentation — a lactic-acid souring of the malt wort (12-16 h, lactic acid bacteria reaching 8.8-9.9 log CFU/mL, pH ~3.0-3.8) followed by an alcoholic fermentation (9-14 h) on indigenous yeast. Dominant lactic acid bacteria are Limosilactobacillus (Lactobacillus) fermentum, Pediococcus acidilactici, Lactococcus lactis and Leuconostoc spp.; the dominant yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae (45-99%). Production is back-slopped: part of a previous batch, or a sun-dried indigenous yeast leaven, seeds the next. DOI 10.3389/fsufs.2021.672410. Underpins the beer-sorghum-trad fermentation archetype. Synthesises the primary measurements of Sawadogo-Lingani et al. (2007).
documents.doesNotSupport: Any pitched pure-culture rate, or European farmhouse grain ferments (a different tradition grouped under the same archetype); it documents West African sorghum beer specifically.

documents.title: The microbiome of Chinese rice wine (Huangjiu)
documents.supports: The microbiology of huangjiu (Chinese yellow rice wine): wheat qu is the starter, supplying amylase, protease and esterase that saccharify grain starch to glucose while Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments it to ethanol — simultaneous saccharification and alcoholic fermentation, termed semi-solid open fermentation. Dominant fungi are S. cerevisiae, Aspergillus oryzae, Rhizopus oryzae and Monascus purpureus; dominant bacteria are Lactobacillus and Bacillus spp., Weissella and Leuconostoc. A typical course ferments at ~30 C for 5-7 days, then the mash is opened to drop to ~15 C and held 1-2 months. Published in Current Research in Food Science, 5, 325-335; DOI 10.1016/j.crfs.2022.01.007. Underpins the huangjiu-qu fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Baijiu solid-state fermentation, Japanese koji sake, or any pitch rate — huangjiu is inoculated with a qu starter culture, not a measured cell count.

documents.title: Microbial Diversity and Volatile Flavor Changes during Gayangju Fermentation, a Traditional Korean House Rice Wine
documents.supports: The microbiology of traditional Korean rice wine made with nuruk. Nuruk is produced by natural solid fermentation of moistened ground rice or wheat, growing a mixed population of moulds (Aspergillus, Rhizopus, Mucor spp.), yeasts (Saccharomyces, Pichia, Candida and others) and lactic acid bacteria; its moulds release amylase and glucoamylase to saccharify the rice while yeasts ferment the released sugars. Through fermentation Saccharomyces cerevisiae exceeded 90% of the fungal community alongside Saccharomycopsis fibuligera, with Lactilactobacillus curvatus, Liquorilactobacillus satsumensis and Pediococcus acidilactici predominant among bacteria. The gayangju course ran at ~25 C for the fermentation stages then ~15 C for roughly 35 days of aging. Published in Foods 11(17):2604; DOI 10.3390/foods11172604. Underpins the korean-nuruk fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A pitch rate (nuruk is a starter culture, not a measured cell count), or Chinese qu / Japanese koji ferments, which are distinct traditions.

documents.title: Genetic diversity of Amylomyces rouxii from ragi tapai in Java Island based on ribosomal regions ITS1/ITS2 and D1/D2
documents.supports: The composition and function of ragi tapai, the Southeast Asian rice starter cake: a dry culture of rice flour, spices and mixed microorganisms, typically circular at about 2.5 cm across and 0.5 cm thick. Amylomyces rouxii is the principal amylolytic organism, producing amyloglucosidase and growing on raw substrate (the study also found some isolates previously identified as A. rouxii are in fact Mucor indicus). The community further includes Rhizopus oryzae, Mucor spp., Endomycopsis burtonii, Candida utilis, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and lactic acid bacteria (Pediococcus pentosaceus, Lactobacillus plantarum, L. fermentum). Fermentation runs on two functional groups: one breaks starch down to glucose, the other converts glucose to ethanol. Published in Mycobiology 50(2):132-141; DOI 10.1080/12298093.2022.2028436. Underpins the rice-ragi fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A pitch rate, or the microbiology of Chinese qu, Korean nuruk or Japanese koji ferments — related traditions with their own starter cultures.

documents.title: Wine Yeast FAQs
documents.supports: The distributor's active-dry-yeast inoculation rates: 2 lb/1000 gal (25 g/hL) for a standard primary fermentation, increasing to 2.8 lb/1000 gal (35 g/hL) for high-Brix juice above 25 degrees Brix. Applied here to the cider-cultured archetype, which doses by weight per volume exactly as wine does; it corroborates the AWRI 25 g/hL wine standard.
documents.doesNotSupport: A resulting viable-cell concentration per mL — the page does not state one, and the 5x10^6 cells/mL target this project uses comes from AWRI. It also supports no rehydration temperature or procedure, which are cited to AWRI instead.

documents.title: The Role of Keeving in Modulating Fermentation and the Flavour Profiles of Apple Brandy
documents.supports: The mechanism of keeving (defecation) in traditional cider: calcium chloride and pectin methylesterase are added to the must; demethylation of the homogalacturonan chain in pectin allows calcium binding and gel formation, and CO2 floats that gel to the surface as the chapeau brun within roughly 2-6 days of fermentation. Close to 50% of the pectin and nutrients are trapped in the gel and the sediment left after decanting, and the resulting shortage of assimilable nitrogen slows the fermentation and arrests it spontaneously. Published in Biomolecules 14(10):1322; DOI 10.3390/biom14101322. Underpins the cider-wild-keeving archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Which indigenous yeast species dominate traditional French keeved cider — the study compared spontaneous fermentation against a pitched S. cerevisiae strain and did not characterise the traditional indigenous population — nor any pitch rate, since keeved cider is not pitched.

documents.title: Isolation and Identification of Indigenous Wine Yeasts and Their Use in Alcoholic Fermentation
documents.supports: The yeast succession of spontaneous (uninoculated) wine fermentation: it begins on the non-Saccharomyces yeasts prevailing on grape skins — Hanseniaspora, Starmerella, Pichia, Debaryomyces and Metschnikowia — which ferment sugar only weakly. The exponential growth phase of Hanseniaspora, Candida and Pichia lasts two to three days before stationary phase, after which S. cerevisiae, more ethanol-tolerant and able to grow anaerobically, dominates and completes the fermentation. The indigenous non-Saccharomyces phase emphasises terroir and produces higher alcohols, esters, terpenes and volatile thiols. Published in Food Technology and Biotechnology 58(3):337-347; DOI 10.17113/ftb.58.03.20.6677. Underpins the wine-native fermentation archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any pitch or inoculation rate — this is the uninoculated case — and no claim about cider, beer or other spontaneous ferments.

documents.title: Flor Yeast: New Perspectives Beyond Wine Aging
documents.supports: The biology of flor yeast and the biological ageing of sherry-type wines: the velum is an air-liquid biofilm formed by film-forming Saccharomyces cerevisiae once any fermentable carbon source is exhausted; increased FLO11 expression at the diauxic shift raises cell-surface hydrophobicity and drives biofilm formation, and the yeast switches from fermentative to oxidative metabolism, consuming ethanol as well as glycerol and acetic and lactic acid. Historical classification recognised four flor races (S. cerevisiae var. beticus, cheresiensis, montuliensis and rouxii), which modern genetic analysis shows share a common origin. Published in Frontiers in Microbiology 7:503; DOI 10.3389/fmicb.2016.00503. Underpins the wine-flor archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A quantitative ethanol range for velum formation — the paper notes only that ethanol sensitivity is inversely correlated with the rate of biofilm formation, so the 15% vol minimum this project records is cited to OIV instead. It also does not discuss the solera system.

documents.title: International Code of Oenological Practices, Part I Definitions — Special Wines
documents.publisher: International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV)
documents.supports: The intergovernmental definitions behind the fortified and flor archetypes. Liqueur wine: acquired alcoholic strength at or above 15% and at or below 22% vol (states may permit up to 24% domestically), made from grape musts including partially fermented musts and/or wine, with distillates, spirits and alcohol of vitivinicultural origin added, optionally with concentrated or caramelised grape must, over-ripened or raisined grapes, mistelles or caramel. Flor or film wines: wines biologically aged in contact with air through the development of a film of typical yeasts on the free surface of the wine, AFTER complete alcoholic fermentation of the must, with wine spirit or neutral alcohol optionally added and the finished wine required to reach at least 15% vol actual alcohol.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any microbiological detail about how the flor velum forms, or any pitch/inoculation rate; it is a definitional standard, not a process manual.

documents.title: International Code of Oenological Practices — Fortification
documents.publisher: International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV)
documents.supports: The OIV definition of fortification: the addition to wines of wine spirit, rectified alcohol of viticultural origin or rectified food alcohol, either to raise alcohol content or to produce special wines (flor/film wines, fortified wines), mistelles and must- or wine-based beverages. The spirit or alcohol used must comply with the production conditions the Code fixes for those products. OIV recommends against fortification undertaken merely to increase alcoholic strength, while permitting it for the special-wine categories.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any specific alcoholic-strength limit (those are in the Special Wines definitions) or the timing of the spirit addition within a given regional style such as port.

documents.title: International Code of Oenological Practices — Special Wines: Sparkling Wines
documents.publisher: International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV)
documents.supports: What the OIV permits for the second fermentation of sparkling wine: a tirage liqueur of sugar, must or concentrated must, plus a selected yeast inoculum, clarifying agents (bentonites, organic fining agents, tannins, potassium alginate) and fermentation activators. Nutritive salts are capped at a maximum dose of 0.3 g/L of diammonium phosphate or ammonium sulphate (expressed as the salt) and 0.6 mg/L of thiamin hydrochloride (expressed as thiamin), classified as processing aids to assist yeast multiplication during secondary fermentation in bottle or closed tank. The bottle route comprises base-wine/cuvee preparation, tirage liqueur preparation, yeast inoculation, clarifying-agent addition, tirage, stacking, riddling, disgorging and dosage.
documents.doesNotSupport: A yeast inoculation rate for tirage, or a required bottle CO2 pressure — the pages consulted state neither.

documents.title: Saccharomyces cerevisiae in the Production of Whisk(e)y
documents.supports: How a whisky wash is fermented for congeners rather than neutrality. Scotch whisky fermentation normally has no temperature control: the wort is pitched at 16-19 C and allowed to rise, typically peaking around 32-33 C, over 2-3 days depending on distillery capacity. The wort is never boiled, so residual malt enzymes keep converting during fermentation, worth roughly 30% additional spirit. Over 100 esters form, predominantly fruity, and iso-amyl alcohol makes up 40-70% of the total higher alcohols, becoming unpleasant at high levels. Most Scotch malt distilleries add commercially supplied cream yeast directly without propagation, while grain distilleries pitch at much lower rates. Limited lactic-acid-bacteria activity is an essential part of the craft of malt distilling: LAB acids esterify to compounds such as ethyl lactate and gamma-dodecalactone giving sweet, fruity and creamy notes. Published in Beverages 2(4):38; DOI 10.3390/beverages2040038. Underpins the spirit-congener-grain archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A numeric pitching rate in cells/mL or g/hL — the paper describes cream-yeast practice and relative rates without giving a figure — nor the fermentation of rum, agave or neutral spirit.

documents.title: Processes, Challenges and Optimisation of Rum Production from Molasses—A Contemporary Review
documents.supports: Rum fermentation from molasses. Fermentation runs from 20 hours to 21 days: 20-26 hour ferments give lighter rums and ferments beyond 7 days give heavier ones. Temperature is maintained at 28-35 C to optimise yeast growth; S. cerevisiae is the usual production species, works optimally at 20-30 C, requires a minimum water activity of 0.65, and commercial distilling strains tolerate 32-35 C with metabolic activity declining rapidly above that. Molasses is stressful enough that few organisms besides Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Bacillus subtilis survive alongside it; minor contributors include Candida, Debaryomyces, Kluyveromyces, Pichia and Hanseniaspora. Dunder — the volatile-depleted liquid residue left in the stills from previous batches — is routinely added back to the molasses preparation to preserve volatiles and organoleptic continuity. Lactobacillus and Propionibacterium are the predominant bacterial contaminants and produce flavour-active 2,3-butanediol, diacetyl and propionic acid, while inhibiting fermentation at excessive concentrations. Published in Fermentation 7(1):21; DOI 10.3390/fermentation7010021. Underpins the spirit-congener-cane archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: The specific Jamaican muck-pit practice or any high-ester dosing figure, and no pitch rate in cells/mL or g/hL.

documents.title: Unveiling the Microbial Ecology behind Mezcal: A Spirit Drink with a Growing Global Demand
documents.supports: The microbial ecology of agave spirits. Agave pinas are cooked in earthen pit ovens or industrial autoclaves, which sterilises the plant material and hydrolyses its complex carbohydrates into fermentable sugars; cross-contamination begins immediately once the oven is opened, through bare-hand manipulation and unsterilised tools. Mezcal production relies on spontaneous fermentation rather than inoculation, the consortium coming from the environments surrounding the production factories. Dominant yeasts in artisanal spontaneous fermentation are Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Hanseniaspora spp., Candida spp., Torulaspora delbrueckii and Kluyveromyces marxianus, alongside lactic acid bacteria and Leuconostoc mesenteroides. Fermentation generally takes approximately 8 to 20 days. Non-Saccharomyces species and bacteria contribute higher alcohols, acetate esters and ethyl esters with floral and fruity character. Published in Fermentation 8(11):662; DOI 10.3390/fermentation8110662. Underpins the agave archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Industrial tequila's inoculated-fermentation parameters or any pitch rate; it documents the spontaneous artisanal case.

documents.title: Chinese Baijiu: The Perfect Works of Microorganisms
documents.supports: The starter cultures and solid-state fermentation behind baijiu. Daqu is a grain distiller's jiuqu made from wheat, barley and/or peas, classified by production temperature — high-temperature for sauce (Maotai) aroma, medium-temperature for strong aroma, low-temperature for light aroma. Xiaoqu is a simpler starter of rice, sorghum or barley made with traditional Chinese medicines, suited to southern China and generating less heat; in xiaoqu baijiu, saccharification and fermentation are conducted at the same time. In traditional production the microorganisms originate from the production environment, the production workers and the jiuqu rather than deliberate pitching, though modern practice may add isolated functional strains. Dominant fungi are Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Kazachstania, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and Apiotrichum; dominant bacteria are Lactobacillus (organic acids), Bacillus (flavour components) and Clostridium (caproic-acid precursors). For strong-flavoured baijiu the pit mud and its Clostridium spp. produce caproic acid and ethyl caproate. Published in Frontiers in Microbiology 13:919044; DOI 10.3389/fmicb.2022.919044. Underpins the baijiu-qu-ssf archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Huangjiu or Japanese koji fermentation, and no pitch rate — baijiu is a starter-culture solid-state ferment with no measured cell count.

documents.title: Fermented Mare Milk and Its Microorganisms for Human Consumption and Health
documents.supports: The microbiology and composition of fermented mare milk (koumiss/airag). Fermentation is a lactic-acid-bacteria and yeast interaction: LAB mainly acidify the milk while yeasts partly modify titratable acidity. It is started by back-slopping — fresh milk inoculated with a small quantity of already-fermented milk as a natural starter. Lactobacillus helveticus predominates among LAB (78.9% of sequences in one study) and Kluyveromyces marxianus and Saccharomyces cerevisiae are the most common yeasts. Koumiss generally contains about 2% alcohol, 0.5-1.5% lactic acid, 2-4% sugar and 2% fat, with Russian classification distinguishing weak (0.7-1% ethanol), normal (1-1.75%) and strong (1.75-2.5%). Published in Foods 13(3):493; DOI 10.3390/foods13030493. Underpins the milk-kefir archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: Fermentation temperature or duration, and distillation into a spirit — the review states neither, so the arkhi distillation step is cited elsewhere.

documents.title: Preserving edible biodiversity through indigenous dairy emulsions: valorization of traditional milk systems for a resilient future
documents.supports: Traditional Mongolian fermented dairy and its distilled derivative. Tarag is a firm Mongolian yoghurt made by fermenting boiled and cooled cow's or goat's milk with Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens, giving a dense curd at pH 3.6-3.9, and it serves as the base for arkhi, a distilled alcoholic beverage derived from fermented milk. Airag (tsege) is a fermentate of horse or camel milk produced by vigorously agitating the milk in leather sacks or wooden containers for one to two days, which supports lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus helveticus and Lactococcus lactis alongside native yeast activity, giving a slightly effervescent drink of 1-3% ethanol. DOI 10.3389/fnut.2025.1693995. Underpins the milk-distilled archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: The details of the arkhi distillation itself — the paper mentions it only in passing — nor any pitch rate, since the culture is back-slopped.

documents.title: Microbial Composition, Bioactive Compounds, Potential Benefits and Risks Associated with Kombucha: A Concise Review
documents.supports: The composition and method of kombucha fermentation. The SCOBY is a metabolically active symbiotic community of bacteria and yeast that forms a jelly-like cellulose pellicle (zooglea biofilm) at the liquid-air interface. Yeasts include Saccharomyces sp., Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Brettanomyces sp.; acetic acid bacteria include Acetobacter aceti, Komagataeibacter xylinum, Gluconobacter oxydans and Acetobacter pasteurianus. The symbiosis is reciprocal: ethanol produced by yeast helps the bacteria produce acetic acid, and that acetic acid stimulates further yeast ethanol production, which also excludes competing microbes. A representative protocol stirs 50 g sucrose into 1 L boiling water, steeps tea for 5 minutes, cools to 20 C, then inoculates with 24 g SCOBY plus 0.2 L of previously fermented kombucha to lower pH and inhibit unwanted organisms. Optimal fermentation runs 6-14 days. Published in Fermentation 9(5):472; DOI 10.3390/fermentation9050472. Underpins the scoby-symbiotic archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A yeast pitch rate in cells/mL — kombucha is inoculated with a physical pellicle and starter liquid — or the microbiology of any other back-slopped ferment.

documents.title: A Holistic Review on Euro-Asian Lactic Acid Bacteria Fermented Cereals and Vegetables
documents.supports: Kvass and related Euro-Asian lactic-fermented cereal beverages. Kvass is made from fermented barley and rye malt, rye flour and stale rye bread, produced mainly in Russia, Poland and the Baltic states. It undergoes a combined lactic and alcoholic fermentation on a natural mixed flora of Saccharomyces cerevisiae with lactic acid bacteria including Lactobacillus casei and Leuconostoc mesenteroides, and species composition varies considerably with fermentation technique and medium. It contains 1% alcohol or less and is not pasteurised, so live LAB remain in the finished drink. Published in Microorganisms 8(8):1176; DOI 10.3390/microorganisms8081176. Underpins the grain-wild-backslop archetype.
documents.doesNotSupport: A specific back-slopping protocol or inoculation quantity, and no claim about non-European folk grain ferments grouped under the same archetype.

documents.title: Winemaking at Home (Circular 717)
documents.publisher: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension (CAES Field Report)
documents.supports: The land-grant extension method for American home country wine. Covers muscadine grapes (Hunt, Cowart, Scuppernong and Carlos cultivars) plus blackberry, blueberry, raspberry, strawberry, apple, crabapple, peach and plum. The sequence is: crush the fruit to release juice, sterilise with sulfites, adjust acid, tannin and sugar, add activated yeast, run a primary fermentation of 3-7 days with pulp contact for reds, strain, ferment out in sealed secondary vessels, and rack periodically off the sediment. It recommends a true wine yeast such as Montrachet No. 522 and accepts baker's yeast as an alternative. Storage is at 60-70 F and fermentation takes roughly one month. Sulfite dosing is 4 Campden tablets per batch for sterilisation, and one-eighth teaspoon of potassium metabisulfite or one Campden tablet per three gallons at racking and bottling. A must brought to 22% sugar targets approximately 11% alcohol by volume, which is the basis for the 10-12% ABV band on the country-wine entries.
documents.doesNotSupport: Dandelion, elderberry, rhubarb or vegetable wines — the bulletin does not cover them, so those entries carry no numeric targets — nor Concord/labrusca-specific figures beyond the shared method.

documents.title: Muscadine Grapes in the Home Garden
documents.supports: Muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) history and nomenclature. Native to the southeastern United States and cultivated for more than 400 years; Native Americans dried the grapes long before European settlement, and Spanish settlements in Florida were producing muscadine wine as early as 1565. The first recognised cultivar was found in North Carolina before 1760, known first as the Big White Grape and later named Scuppernong; the publication states explicitly that the name became generic for all bronze muscadines and that this is incorrect nomenclature, since Scuppernong is only one of many cultivars. Muscadines have a high tolerance of the pests and diseases that make bunch-grape production nearly impossible in eastern North Carolina, and are popular with native Southerners for wine, pies and jellies. Originally published 30 June 2006, reviewed and revised 11 August 2025.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any winemaking figures — it is a home-garden growing guide; the country-wine method and its targets are cited to UGA Circular 717.

documents.title: Dandelion: What makes this weed so great?
documents.supports: That dandelions are not native to North America: Europeans brought them over in the 1600s deliberately as an edible and medicinal crop rather than as a weed, and the plant has been in continuous use as food and medicine for at least a thousand years, with winemaking among its uses. Context for the dandelion-wine entry.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any recipe, gravity or ABV for dandelion wine — none is published, which is why that entry asserts no numbers.

documents.title: Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method
documents.supports: The qvevri winemaking method as UNESCO documents it. The qvevri is an egg-shaped earthenware vessel used for making, ageing and storing wine. After pressing, the juice, grape skins, stalks and pips are poured into the qvevri, which is sealed and buried in the ground so the wine can ferment for five to six months. Knowledge of qvevri manufacture and of qvevri winemaking is passed down by families, neighbours, friends and relatives, with children learning through observation during communal harvesting, and wine is integral to both secular celebration and religious ritual in Georgia. Inscribed in 2013 (8.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Underpins the qvevri and skin-contact entries in the WINETRAD edition.
documents.doesNotSupport: Any gravity, ABV or analytical target — it documents a living cultural practice, not a product specification — and no claim about Portuguese talha, Spanish tinaja or other clay-vessel traditions.

documents.title: Vin Methode Nature — Charter of Commitment (English, updated January 2022)
documents.publisher: Syndicat de defense des vins naturels (Vin Methode Nature)
documents.supports: The twelve commitments of the French Vin Methode Nature label, whose charter the Syndicat de defense des vins naturels lodged with the DGCCRF and which that authority validated in 2020. Grapes must be 100% certified organic (Nature & Progres, or in the third year of conversion) and hand-harvested. Inoculation of yeast or bacteria is not permitted; a pied de cuve is the permitted route to starting fermentation. Oenological additives and processing aids are not permitted, nor is voluntary modification of the structure of the grapes. Interventionist physical techniques are prohibited, the charter naming reverse osmosis, filtration, thermovinification and centrifugation. Sulphites are the sole exception, permitted in small declared amounts in the finished wine whatever its colour or style, measured by Frantz Paul analysis, with two identification logos separating wines with no added sulphites from wines carrying an addition. Producers sign the Charter of Commitment and are subject to control by the Syndicate.
documents.doesNotSupport: A precise sulphite ceiling in mg/L. The published PDF does not extract its numerals reliably and the label website's stated figures did not agree closely enough with the charter text to commit one, so no sulphite number is asserted anywhere in this archive. It also supports no gravity, ABV or sensory target, and applies only to wines carrying this specific French label, not to natural wine as a general description.

documents.title: VIVC passport data — Cabernet Sauvignon (variety no. 1929)
documents.publisher: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kuhn-Institut
documents.supports: Grape variety identity: prime name, 62 recorded synonyms, species, berry colour, country of origin and pedigree. Retrieved and read as the worked example for the whole catalogue.
documents.doesNotSupport: Harvest chemistry. VIVC carries no Brix, titratable acidity or pH, so it cannot support the numeric fields on this project's 53 wine-grape records. It was evaluated as a replacement for the dead iv.ucdavis.edu citations and deliberately not used for them: swapping a homepage for a per-variety page would have cut 53 from the shallow-link debt while citing a document that does not contain the figures.

documents.title: Hops Companion — A brewer's guide to hop varieties and hop products, 4th edition (2022)
documents.supports: Per-variety specifications for 155 hop varieties: alpha and beta acids (%), cohumulone (% of alpha), total oil (mL/100g) and the myrcene, humulene, caryophyllene, farnesene and linalool fractions (% of total oil), plus total polyphenols, pedigree and aroma descriptors. Retrieved and read; Cascade and Simcoe checked against the page directly.
documents.doesNotSupport: It is a typical-range guide, not a lot analysis — a specific bale is certified by its own certificate of analysis and will differ. The figures in this project's hop records were not imported from this PDF: extracting it programmatically produces plausible but wrong values (Simcoe parsed as 4.5-8.0% alpha against a printed 12.0-15.5%), so the guide is cited as the source that carries each variety's specification, and reconciling the stored numbers against it remains outstanding.
